cells.tense: You're holding what you actually made, and you're not arguing with it.
cells.ask: Offer one finished thing of yours to something undecided — a blank page, an open hour, a question nobody has answered — and let what you've already carried be the ground you stand on while the next thing stays unknown, so you get to find out that what you made can hold your weight.
cells.core:
There's nothing left in it to finish and nothing in you pulling to reopen it. What started as an open possibility is out in the world with your fingerprints on it, and it turns out to be carrying fine. That's not a small thing — plenty of people are still holding the lid on something.

What that leaves you free for is the part with no shape yet. You can walk into what's undecided without bracing, because you've already proven you can carry a thing all the way to its end. So let the whole thing you've made stay whole, and give the open question an hour of your attention with nothing to report back.
cells.sheetLine: What you made is done, and you're holding it without argument.
cells.place: where you move with only enough light for the next step

cells.tense: You're already living past the ending, at a point the work hasn't reached yet.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing nearest to done and mark it done — write the date on it, send it, shut the file — then stop for an hour without starting anything new, so you can find out what the finished thing weighs when you're not already standing a year ahead of it.
cells.core:
Part of a good finish is letting it actually finish. Instead you're gripping toward how it'll be received, what comes after, whether the next thing lands — and the looking-past has gotten wider than the finishing. You're two steps into what comes after while the last step still needs your hands on it.

The weight is real and so is what you've made; nobody's taking that away. But when you check everything one more time and push the ending to where you can see it from a distance, that part isn't yours to steer from here — how it lands happens somewhere you don't get to stand. What's in front of you tonight is just the next ten minutes of it.

cells.tense: The thing you made is a while behind you now, and you're still standing there with it.
cells.ask: Take one walk with no destination — three blocks, turn by what pulls you — and say out loud one thing you notice, so your own voice can tell you something you didn't already know.
cells.core:
The finished thing sits behind you as something you carry without holding it. You look at it, it's real, and you let it count — that's the shape of it working, and it's not far off.

What's happened instead is that the receiving part has gone quiet. You can still see the whole thing, and you can still say it was real, but the part of you that gets to feel it as yours isn't in the room. Effort won't put that back; more producing won't either. What brings it back is smaller — something arriving that you didn't build, and letting it land in you long enough to notice you felt it. One plain thing is enough for today.
cells.sheetLine: Something you made is finished and you keep leaving yourself out of it.

cells.tense: You're the one shaping how this ends, and you talk about it like it's the weather.
cells.ask: Name one decision you made but haven't said out loud — the thing you quietly picked weeks ago — and write it on a note you date and keep, so you can hold your own call in your own hand.
cells.core:
The end of a thing gets said plainly — this is mine, this turned out how it was meant to. That's it working, and the saying is the only part missing.

What's happening instead is the choice got left unnamed. Something got completed and you've been treating it as a fact that arrived instead of a thing you carried to its end — 'it turned out that way' when you're the one who made the last call, and the call was yours.

So don't find a bigger thing to complete. Go smaller: find what you already decided and give it your name, in your own words, on something you'll see again. The real answer is usually something you've been keeping in your pocket, waiting for permission you don't actually need.
cells.sheetLine: You're finishing it, and telling it like it finished itself.
